title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XVII
paragraphs:
“The clerkly person smiled and said
Promise was a pretty maid,
But being poor she died unwed.”

The Reverend Camden Farebrother, whom Lydgate visited the following evening, lived in an old stone parsonage venerable enough to match the church it overlooked. The furniture was old too, though of a different vintage: it belonged to the generations of Mr. Farebrother’s father and grandfather. White-painted chairs bore gilding and wreaths, and remnants of red silk damask survived with splits in them. Engraved portraits of Lord Chancellors and other celebrated lawyers of the previous century hung there, reflected in old pier mirrors, along with little satinwood tables and sofas that resembled extended uncomfortable chairs. All stood out against dark wooden paneling. Such was the appearance of the drawing room into which Lydgate was shown. Three ladies received him, equally old-fashioned and possessed of a faded but genuine respectability. Mrs. Farebrother, the Vicar’s white-haired mother, wore frills and a kerchief with dainty cleanliness; upright and bright-eyed, she was not yet seventy. Her sister, Miss Noble, was a tiny old woman of gentler appearance, her own frills and kerchief noticeably more worn and mended. Miss Winifred Farebrother, the Vicar’s older sister, was good-looking like him, but pinched and subdued as unmarried women often become when they spend their lives continually subject to their elders. Lydgate had not expected so quaint a group. Knowing only that Mr. Farebrother was a bachelor, he had imagined being shown into a snug room furnished chiefly with books and natural-history specimens. The Vicar himself looked somewhat different, as most men do when acquaintances first see them at home. Some resemble actors known for genial roles unfortunately cast as misers in a new play. That was not Mr. Farebrother’s case. He was simply a little gentler and quieter. His mother did most of the talking, while he occasionally added a good-humored qualification. The old lady plainly considered it her habit and duty to tell visitors what to think; no subject was entirely safe without her guidance. Miss Winifred attended to all her small wants, leaving her free to perform this function. Meanwhile, little Miss Noble carried a basket on her arm. Into it she slipped a piece of sugar, first dropping it into her saucer as though by accident, then glancing furtively round and returning to her tea with a small innocent sound like that of a tiny, timid animal. Please do not think badly of Miss Noble. The basket held little portions saved from her more portable food for the children of poor friends whom she trotted off to visit on fine mornings. Caring for and indulging every needy creature delighted her so spontaneously that she regarded it almost as an enjoyable vice to which she was addicted. Perhaps she knew herself tempted to steal from those who had plenty in order to give to those who had nothing, and bore in her conscience the guilt of that suppressed desire. One must be poor to know the luxury of giving!

Mrs. Farebrother welcomed the guest with brisk formality and precision. Soon she informed him that the household seldom needed medical assistance. She had raised her children to wear flannel and not to overeat; overeating, in her view, was the chief reason people required doctors. Lydgate spoke on behalf of those whose parents had overeaten, but Mrs. Farebrother considered that a dangerous view. Nature was more just than that. Any criminal could easily claim that his ancestors should have been hanged instead of him. If people with bad parents were themselves bad, they were hanged for their own badness. There was no need to reach back into what you could not see.
“My mother resembles old George the Third,” said the Vicar. “She disapproves of metaphysics.”

“I disapprove of what is wrong, Camden. Hold fast to a few plain truths, I say, and make everything agree with them. When I was young, Mr. Lydgate, there was never any dispute about right and wrong. We knew our catechism, and that was enough. We learned our creed and our duty. Every respectable member of the Church held the same opinions. Now you may quote the Prayer Book itself and still be contradicted.”
“That must make life quite pleasant for people who enjoy defending their own opinion,” said Lydgate.
“But my mother always gives in,” said the Vicar slyly.

“No, no, Camden. You mustn’t give Mr. Lydgate a false impression of ME. I shall never disrespect my parents by abandoning what they taught me. Anyone can see where changing leads. Change once, and why not twenty times?”
“A man might find good reasons to change once without finding reasons to change again,” said Lydgate, amused by the decisive old lady.

“Excuse me. If you rely on arguments, a man without a steady mind will always find plenty. My father never changed. He preached plain moral sermons without arguments, and he was a good man—few were better. When you can produce a good man out of arguments, I’ll produce a good dinner by reading you the cookbook. That’s my opinion, and I think anyone’s stomach will support it.”
“Certainly about the dinner, mother,” said Mr. Farebrother.

“It’s the same principle, whether a dinner or a man. I’m nearly seventy, Mr. Lydgate, and I rely on experience. I’m not likely to follow new lights, though there are plenty here as elsewhere. They came in, I say, with those mixed fabrics that neither wash nor wear properly. It wasn’t like that when I was young. A Churchman was a Churchman, and you could be fairly sure a clergyman was a gentleman, if nothing more. Now he may be no better than a Dissenter and try to push my son aside on some pretext of doctrine. But whoever wants to push him aside, I’m proud to say, Mr. Lydgate, that he can stand comparison with any preacher in the kingdom, let alone this town. That’s a low enough standard—at least to my mind, since I was born and raised in Exeter.”
“Mothers are never biased,” said Mr. Farebrother with a smile. “What do you suppose Tyke’s mother says about him?”
“Ah, poor woman! What indeed?” said Mrs. Farebrother, her sharpness momentarily blunted by her faith in mothers’ judgments. “Depend on it, she tells herself the truth.”
“And what is the truth?” Lydgate asked. “I’d be interested to know.”
“Oh, nothing bad,” said Mr. Farebrother. “He’s a zealous fellow. Not very learned, and not very wise, I think—because I disagree with him.”
“But Camden!” said Miss Winifred. “Only today Griffin and his wife told me Mr. Tyke said they would receive no more coal if they came to hear you preach.”

Mrs. Farebrother put down the knitting she had resumed after her modest portion of tea and toast, and looked at her son as if to say, “Do you hear that?” Miss Noble murmured, “Oh, poor things, poor things!” Probably she meant the double loss of sermons and coal. But the Vicar answered calmly:
“That’s because they aren’t my parishioners. And I don’t think my sermons are worth a load of coal to them.”

“Mr. Lydgate,” said Mrs. Farebrother, unable to let that pass, “you don’t know my son. He always undervalues himself. I tell him he’s undervaluing the God who made him, and made him an excellent preacher.”
“I think that’s my cue to take Mr. Lydgate to the study, mother,” the Vicar said, laughing. Turning to Lydgate, he added, “I promised to show you my collection. Shall we go?”

All three ladies protested. Mr. Lydgate must not be hurried away without the chance of another cup of tea. Miss Winifred had plenty of good tea in the pot. Why was Camden so eager to drag a visitor to his den? There was nothing there but preserved vermin and drawers full of bluebottles and moths, and not even a carpet. Mr. Lydgate must forgive it. A game of cribbage would be much better. In short, a vicar could plainly be adored by the women of his household as the king of men and preachers while still being thought greatly in need of their guidance. With the usual shallowness of a young bachelor, Lydgate wondered why Mr. Farebrother had not taught them better.

“My mother isn’t used to visitors taking an interest in my hobbies,” said the Vicar as he opened his study door. The room was indeed as bare of bodily comforts as the ladies had suggested, unless one counted a short porcelain pipe and a tobacco box.

“Men in your profession don’t usually smoke,” he said. Lydgate smiled and shook his head. “Nor in mine, properly speaking, I suppose. You’ll hear Bulstrode and Company count that pipe against me. They don’t know how pleased the devil would be if I gave it up.”
“I understand. You’re excitable and need something calming. I’m more sluggish; it would make me lazy. I’d fling myself into idleness and stagnate with all my strength.”

“And you intend to give all that strength to your work. I’m ten or twelve years older and have reached a compromise. I feed a weakness or two to keep them from clamoring. Look,” the Vicar continued, opening several small drawers. “I believe I’ve made a complete study of the district’s insects. I’m continuing with both animals and plants, but at least I’ve done the insects properly. We’re unusually rich in orthoptera. I don’t know whether—ah! You’ve picked up that glass jar. You’re looking at that instead of my drawers. You don’t really care for these things?”

“Not compared with this wonderful specimen without a brain. I’ve never had time to devote much attention to natural history. Structure caught my interest early, and it lies directly within my profession. I have no other hobby. There’s an entire sea for me to swim in there.”

“Ah, you’re a fortunate man,” said Mr. Farebrother, turning on his heel and beginning to fill his pipe. “You don’t know what it is to need tobacco for the spirit: bad corrections of ancient texts, or little notes on a variety of Aphis Brassicae, signed with the familiar name Philomicron, for the ‘Twaddler’s Magazine.’ Or a learned study of insects in the Pentateuch, including all those not mentioned but probably encountered by the Israelites crossing the desert; with a monograph on Solomon’s treatment of the ant, demonstrating the agreement between Proverbs and modern research. You don’t mind being smoked, do you?”

Lydgate was more surprised by this frankness than by its implication that the Vicar felt he had not quite found his proper calling. The neatly fitted drawers and shelves and the bookcase full of expensive illustrated works on natural history made him think again of the card winnings and where they went. But he was beginning to wish that the most favorable interpretation of everything Mr. Farebrother did would prove the true one. The Vicar’s candor did not seem the repellent kind that arises from an uneasy conscience trying to anticipate other people’s judgment. It seemed simply the relief of wanting as little pretense as possible. Apparently he realized that he might seem to be speaking too freely so soon, for presently he said:

“I haven’t told you that I have an advantage, Mr. Lydgate: I know you better than you know me. Do you remember Trawley, who shared your rooms in Paris for a while? We corresponded, and he told me a good deal about you. When you first arrived, I wasn’t certain you were the same man. I was very pleased to discover you were. But I haven’t forgotten that you’ve had no similar introduction to me.”

Lydgate sensed a delicacy of feeling behind this, but scarcely understood it. “What has become of Trawley, by the way?” he asked. “I’ve lost touch entirely. He was enthusiastic about French social theories and talked of going to the American backwoods to found a sort of Pythagorean community. Did he go?”
“Not at all. He’s practicing at a German spa and has married a wealthy patient.”

“Then my ideas have lasted better so far,” said Lydgate with a short, scornful laugh. “He insisted that medicine was inevitably a system of humbug. I said the fault lay with the men who bowed to lies and foolishness. Rather than denouncing the humbug from outside the walls, it might be better to install some disinfecting equipment inside. In short, since I’m reporting my own conversation, you may be sure all the good sense was on my side.”

“Your plan is considerably harder to carry out than a Pythagorean community, though. You face not only the old Adam within yourself, but all the descendants of the original Adam who make up the society around you. You see, I’ve paid twelve or thirteen years more than you for my knowledge of difficulties. But—” Mr. Farebrother paused, then added, “you’re looking at that glass jar again. Would you like an exchange? You won’t get it without a fair trade.”
“I have some sea mice, excellent specimens, preserved in spirits. And I’ll add Robert Brown’s new work, ‘Microscopic Observations on the Pollen of Plants,’ unless you already have it.”

“Considering how much you want the specimen, I might ask more. Suppose I make you examine my drawers and agree with me about all my new species?” While he spoke, the Vicar alternated between walking about with his pipe in his mouth and returning to hover affectionately over his drawers. “Good training for a young doctor who has to please patients in Middlemarch. You must learn to be bored, remember. Still, you may have the specimen on your own terms.”

“Don’t you think men exaggerate the need to indulge everyone’s nonsense until the very fools they indulge despise them?” said Lydgate. He moved beside Mr. Farebrother and looked rather distractedly at the insects, arranged in fine gradations and labeled in exquisite handwriting. “The shortest way is to make people feel your value. Then they have to put up with you, whether you flatter them or not.”

“I agree entirely. But you must be sure you have that value, and you must remain independent. Very few men manage it. Either you slip out of service altogether and become useless, or you wear the harness and are pulled a long way in the direction your teammates take. But do look at these delicate orthoptera!”
In the end Lydgate had to examine every drawer. The Vicar laughed at himself but persisted with the display.

“About what you said of wearing a harness,” Lydgate began when they were seated, “I decided some time ago to wear as little as possible. That’s why I resolved not to attempt anything in London, for many years at least. I disliked what I saw while studying there: so much empty self-importance and obstructive maneuvering. People in the country make fewer claims to knowledge and offer less companionship, but for that very reason they touch one’s pride less. One breeds less resentment and can follow one’s own course more peacefully.”

“Yes, well, you’ve made a good beginning. You’re in the right profession, doing the work you feel best suited for. Some people miss that and regret it too late. But don’t be too certain you’ll keep your independence.”
“Do you mean family ties?” Lydgate asked, imagining that those might press rather heavily on Mr. Farebrother.

“Not entirely. They certainly make many things harder. But a good wife, a good woman without worldly ambitions, can really help a man and preserve his independence. One of my parishioners is a fine fellow, but he would scarcely have pulled through as he has without his wife. Do you know the Garths? I don’t think they were Peacock’s patients.”
“No, though there’s a Miss Garth at old Featherstone’s in Lowick.”
“Their daughter. An excellent girl.”
“She’s very quiet. I’ve hardly noticed her.”
“You may be certain she’s noticed you.”
“I don’t understand,” said Lydgate. He could hardly say, “Of course.”
“Oh, she takes everyone’s measure. I prepared her for confirmation. She’s a favorite of mine.”

Mr. Farebrother smoked silently for a few moments. Lydgate had no desire to hear more about the Garths. At last the Vicar put down his pipe, stretched out his legs, and turned his bright eyes towards Lydgate with a smile.
“But we Middlemarch people aren’t as tame as you imagine. We have our intrigues and factions. I belong to a faction, for example, and so does Bulstrode. If you vote for me, you’ll offend him.”
“What is there against Bulstrode?” Lydgate asked emphatically.
“I didn’t say there was anything against him except that. Vote against him, and you’ll make an enemy of him.”

“I don’t know that I need worry about that,” said Lydgate rather proudly. “But he seems to have good ideas about hospitals and spends large sums on useful public causes. He could help me considerably in carrying out my plans. As for his religious beliefs—well, as Voltaire said, incantations will kill a flock of sheep if accompanied by a certain quantity of arsenic. I’m looking for the man who will supply the arsenic. His incantations don’t concern me.”

“Very well. But then you mustn’t offend your arsenic supplier. You won’t offend me, you know,” said Mr. Farebrother with complete sincerity. “I don’t turn my own convenience into other people’s duties. I disagree with Bulstrode on many things. I dislike his circle. They’re narrow and ignorant, and do more to make their neighbors uncomfortable than to improve them. Their system is a kind of clique combining worldly and spiritual interests. They really regard the rest of humanity as a condemned carcass on which they can feed themselves for heaven. But,” he added with a smile, “I’m not saying his new hospital is a bad thing. As for his wanting to push me out of the old one, if he thinks I’m harmful, he’s only returning the compliment. And I’m no model clergyman, merely a tolerable substitute.”

Lydgate was not certain the Vicar was judging himself unfairly. A model clergyman, like a model doctor, ought to consider his profession the finest in the world and treat all knowledge as nourishment for his understanding and treatment of moral disease. He merely asked, “What reason does Bulstrode give for replacing you?”

“That I don’t teach his opinions, which he calls spiritual religion, and that I have no time to spare. Both are true. But I could make time, and I would welcome the forty pounds. That’s the plain truth. Still, let’s drop it. I only meant to say that, if you vote for your arsenic supplier, you mustn’t avoid me afterwards. I can’t spare you. You’re like a traveler who has circled the world and settled among us; you’ll keep alive my belief that the other side of the globe exists. Now tell me all about Paris.”
